Chapter Six. Coming Home to a Changed World.
Coming home—it’s supposed to bring relief, right? A chance to finally leave the war behind, and maybe start fresh. But for so many, stepping off that plane is just the start of a whole new battle. Everything looks the same, but nothing feels quite right. Family and friends try so hard to welcome you back, but there’s this distance—something no one wants to name, but everyone feels.
There’s a story I want to share with you. It’s about a woman who spent months working in a detention facility overseas. When she finally made it home, she couldn’t even sleep in her own bed. The quiet in her childhood house, the place that once felt so safe, now felt suffocating—almost too much after all the noise and tension of the base.
She tried to get back to her old routines. You know, coffee with her mom, walks with her dog. But those memories? They just wouldn’t let go. Sometimes, out of nowhere, a car would backfire and she’d flinch. Or she’d catch herself scanning crowds, looking for threats that weren’t there.
The toughest part? Conversations with people she loved. Everyone wanted to understand what it had been like. But how do you even begin to explain what you’ve seen—or the choices you had to make? When the questions came—Did you hurt anyone? Did you see anything awful?—she’d just shake her head, change the subject, or tell a version of the story that felt safer. Sometimes, it’s just easier to let people believe you’re fine.
Here’s something a lot of folks don’t realize—coming home when you’ve changed is hard in ways nobody expects. The world expects you to go back to who you were, but that person isn’t there anymore. The instincts that kept you alive don’t really fit back into everyday life. And the guilt, or the shame? That can make it tough to trust yourself, never mind trusting anyone else.
Some veterans found comfort with each other. Maybe you’ve seen them—gathering at a bar or in a support group, sharing stories only they truly get. There’s some relief in not feeling alone, but it can also feel like being stuck—tied together by things that make you feel separate from the rest of the world.
The challenge of adjusting isn’t just about trauma or regret. It’s really about learning to live with everything that happened—and trying to make sense of a world that sometimes just doesn’t make sense anymore. And for a lot of folks, maybe the hardest part is realizing that the war never really leaves you. It stays with you, shaping your life in ways you never imagined.
